title: Held down, never killed
hookLine: under the planted foot lies a small figure, ignorance itself, and the dancer never finishes him off
carry: the real enemy is ignorance, held down by remembering
tomorrow: why is there a river in Shiva's hair?

cards: He's the easiest part of the image to miss. Look down past the swinging arms and the flying hair to Nataraja's right foot, the planted one.
Under it, flat on his belly, lies a small, round-limbed figure, often holding a snake, pinned to the ground. He isn't the hero of anything.
He's closer to the name that was right there a second ago, or the reason you walked into this room: gone. Small, daily, and always back. His name is Apasmara.

teach.b: In the usual reading, Apasmara is ignorance: the forgetting that hides what's true.
Hindu teachers have a word for it, avidya, not-knowing, and in much of Hindu thought it's the root trouble, deeper than any enemy outside you: forgetting who you really are, and forgetting God.
There's a story behind him, told in the temple tradition of Chidambaram and retold by the art historian Ananda Coomaraswamy.

teach.h: TIGER, SNAKE, DWARF FROM THE SAGES.
teach.b: In a forest lived a community of sages, proud of their own rites, who thought they had no need of Shiva. He came among them in disguise, and they were furious, so they used their powers against him.
First they sent a tiger. Shiva caught it, peeled off its skin, and wore it at his waist. Then a snake: he hung it around his neck like a garland.
Then a dwarf, a malicious little creature. Shiva put his foot on its back and began to dance, and the sages, watching, gave up their pride. Here's the detail worth keeping.
Shiva never kills Apasmara. He keeps him under the foot, and keeps dancing. Many teachers read that as honest: ignorance doesn't vanish for good in one blow.

teach.h: HE IS HELD DOWN, NEVER KILLED.
teach.b: It's held down, again and again, by remembering.
That's why so much Hindu practice is repetition: a name said on every bead of a mala, a lamp lit every evening, the same prayer before every meal. Each one is the foot pressing down again.
Remembering isn't a victory you win once.

teach.h: REMEMBERING IS A STEP YOU KEEP TAKING.
teach.b: It's a step you keep taking.

how: In Nataraja images the right foot rests on Apasmara, a small figure read as ignorance or forgetfulness; the story of the forest sages, the tiger, the snake and the dwarf is told in the temple tradition of Chidambaram. Repeated practices, such as japa on a mala and the daily lamp, are often explained as remembering again and again.

o: a dance where Shiva crushes and kills a demon for good
Shiva the dancer, here his foot holding forgetting down

games.q: under the foot — tap the pairs.
p: its skin worn at the waist

s: he keeps him under the foot and keeps dancing. forgetting is held down, never destroyed.
the forest sages sent a tiger, a snake and a dwarf against Shiva
he wore the tiger's skin and the snake, and danced on the dwarf.
in much of Hindu thought, the root trouble is an enemy outside you
it's avidya, ignorance: forgetting who you are and forgetting God. held down by remembering.

games.q: you're the dancer. the sages have sent a malicious dwarf against you, and now he's under your foot. what do you do?
o: crush him once and for all.
keep him under your foot and dance.
games.why: Shiva keeps Apasmara pinned and dances. some readers say forgetting can't be finished off once; it has to be held down again and again.

practice: With both feet flat on the floor, rest your attention in the right foot: the heel, the ball, the toes.
When the mind wanders off into a plan or a memory, that's Apasmara, and it's fine: press the right foot gently into the floor and come back.
If you pray, say Shiva's name, or the name of God you use, each time you come back, the way a mala is told bead by bead; if not, just say here.

wordCard.voice: Apasmara, under the planted foot: ignorance, avidya, held down and never killed, so that remembering stays a step the dancer keeps taking.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Apasmara, the figure under Nataraja's foot, read as forgetfulness and ignorance.

carryVoice: Your line: the real enemy is ignorance, held down by remembering. When forgetting comes back, press down again, gently. See you tomorrow.
